title: Cross-Validation of Open-Source Quantum Network Simulators
authors: Joaquin Chung, Michal Hajdušek, Naphan Benchasattabuse, Robert J. Hayek, Alexander Kolar, Ansh Singal, Kento Samuel Soon, Kentaro Teramoto, Allen Zang, Caitao Zhan, Raj Kettimuthu, Rodney Van Meter
abstract: We present a comparative analysis of two open-source quantum network simulators, QuISP and SeQUeNCe, focusing on cross-validation of basic networking tasks to ensure consistency and accuracy in simulation outputs. Although both simulators are designed to study quantum network management policies and their dynamics under complex noise models, their differing underlying assumptions can lead to variations in simulation results. We highlight the discrepancies in how the two simulators handle connections, internal network node processing time, and classical communication, resulting in significant quantitative and qualitative differences in the time required to perform basic network tasks such as entanglement generation, purification, and swapping. We simulate common scenarios between the simulators to compare both the latency of resource distribution and the fidelity of the distributed resources. Our findings indicate that while the simulators differ in the time required to complete network tasks---a constant factor difference attributable to their respective connection models---they agree on the fidelity of the distributed resources under identical error parameters. This work demonstrates a crucial first step towards enhancing the reliability and reproducibility of quantum network simulations, as well as leading to full protocol development. Furthermore, our benchmarking methodology establishes a foundational set of tasks for the cross-validation of simulators to study future quantum networks.
summary: This paper compares two open-source quantum network simulators, QuISP and SeQUeNCe, by cross-validating basic tasks like entanglement generation and purification. The authors find that while the simulators disagree on the time taken for these tasks, they correctly predict the final resource fidelity under the same noise conditions. This work establishes a vital benchmark for improving the reliability of quantum network simulations.
main_problem: To ensure the consistency and accuracy of simulation outputs when modeling quantum network tasks across different open-source simulators.
main_result: The simulators show quantitative differences in task completion time due to connection models, but they agree on the final fidelity of distributed resources under identical error parameters.
method: A comparative analysis (cross-validation) was performed by simulating fundamental quantum networking primitives like entanglement generation, swapping, and purification using two distinct simulators.
model_or_system: The study models quantum networks, which utilize photonic qubits and quantum memories to distribute entanglement over long distances, simulating first-generation (1G) repeater protocols.
key_observables: Latency of resource distribution (time required for tasks) and the fidelity of the distributed entangled resources.
important_parameters: Error parameters (e.g., Pauli noise, qubit loss), connection model assumptions, and classical communication timing.
main_assumptions: The comparison assumes that the core physics of resource fidelity is correctly modeled, even if the timing mechanics differ between simulators.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the three core processes: link-level entanglement generation (MIM), entanglement swapping at a repeater node, and entanglement purification.
paper_structure: The paper establishes a comparative framework by detailing the simulation of basic quantum networking tasks, comparing the results from QuISP and SeQUeNCe, and concluding with a methodology for future cross-validation.
why_interesting: It provides a rigorous benchmarking methodology for quantum network simulators, which is crucial for developing reliable protocols for future quantum internet architectures.
